sections.preamble: You are a coding assistant running inside pi, a coding agent harness. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

Additional tools may be available.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for targeted changes. Batch changes to one file in a single call.
- Each edits[].oldText must exactly and uniquely match the original file. Keep matches short and non-overlapping; merge nearby changes without including large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

1. According to the traditional date fixed by Roman scholars, the city was founded in 753 BC.
2. Legend says Romulus and Remus were suckled by a she-wolf on the Palatine Hill.
3. Romulus killed his brother and became the city's first king.
4. Early Rome grew up on the best ford of the Tiber, near a low island in the river.
5. The seven hills formed the original urban core of the settlement.
6. The Etruscans to the north shaped early Roman religion, engineering, and royal regalia.
7. The Cloaca Maxima, a great sewer dug in the royal period, still carries water today.
8. Seven kings traditionally ruled Rome, from Romulus to Tarquinius Superbus.
9. Servius Tullius, the sixth king, is credited with the earliest defensive wall of the city.
10. The last king, Tarquin the Proud, was expelled in 509 BC after the outrage against Lucretia.
11. The Republic replaced kings with annually elected magistrates who served for one year.
12. Two consuls shared supreme command and could block one another's decisions.
13. The Senate, a council of elders and ex-magistrates, became the enduring heart of Roman politics.
14. Aristocratic clans were called patricians and everyone else was a plebeian.
15. In 494 BC the plebeians marched to the Sacred Mount and won their own tribunes.
16. Tribunes of the plebs could veto any magistrate's act and were legally sacrosanct.
17. The Twelve Tables of 451 BC gave Rome its first written body of law.
18. The Licinian-Sextian laws of 367 BC opened the consulship to plebeian candidates.
19. Gallic invaders under Brennus sacked the city around 390 BC.
20. The geese of Juno were said to have alerted the defenders of the Capitol during that siege.
21. Rome bound its Latin neighbors together with a web of unequal alliances.
22. The Samnite Wars of the late fourth century gave Rome control of central Italy.
23. The Appian Way was begun in 312 BC to move legions and officials southward.
24. Pyrrhus of Epirus beat Rome at Heraclea and Asculum, but lost irreplaceable men each time.
25. His remark that one more such victory would ruin him gave us the phrase "Pyrrhic victory."
26. The fall of Tarentum in 272 BC ended Greek resistance in peninsular Italy.
27. The First Punic War began in 264 BC and forced Rome to build a fleet from scratch.
28. By 241 BC Carthage had lost at sea, and Sicily became Rome's first overseas province.
29. Hannibal led an army, including war elephants, over the Alps in 218 BC.
30. At Cannae in 216 BC he encircled a Roman army and killed tens of thousands in a single day.
31. Fabius Maximus earned the nickname Cunctator for refusing pitched battle.
32. Scipio Africanus learned Hannibal's tactics during hard campaigning in Spain.
33. His capture of New Carthage in 209 BC broke Carthaginian power on the continent.
34. The Battle of Zama in 202 BC ended the Second Punic War.
35. Within a century of Zama, Rome had turned the eastern Mediterranean into provinces.
36. Corinth was razed in 146 BC, the same year Carthage was destroyed.
37. The territory of Carthage became the rich province of Africa.
38. Tiberius Gracchus was beaten to death in 133 BC for trying to redistribute public land.
39. His brother Gaius pushed broader reforms a decade later and met the same fate.
40. Marius opened the legions to landless citizens in 107 BC.
41. That reform created soldiers whose careers depended on their generals rather than on the state.
42. The Jugurthine War exposed how thoroughly money could buy Roman politics in North Africa.
43. Marius annihilated the Cimbri and Teutones at Vercellae in 101 BC.
44. The Social War of 91 BC ended with Rome granting citizenship to its Italian allies.
45. Sulla marched a Roman legion on Rome itself in 88 BC, shattering centuries of taboo.
46. His dictatorship was followed by proscription lists that outlawed and executed hundreds of nobles.
47. Sulla laid down his dictatorship in 79 BC and died in retirement soon after.
48. Spartacus led a slave army that defeated Roman forces for two years from 73 BC.
49. Crassus crushed the revolt, though Pompey claimed much of the credit.
50. Pompey cleared the Mediterranean of pirates in about three months in 67 BC.
51. The first triumvirate quietly divided influence among Pompey, Crassus, and Caesar in 60 BC.
52. Caesar spent nine years conquering Gaul as far as the Rhine.
53. Those campaigns are known chiefly from Caesar's own crisp commentaries.
54. Crassus died at Carrhae in 53 BC as Parthian horse archers destroyed his legions.
55. Caesar crossed the Rubicon in January 49 BC and started a new civil war.
56. Pompey fled east and was murdered in Egypt after Caesar won at Pharsalus in 48 BC.
57. Senators stabbed Caesar to death on the Ides of March, 44 BC.
58. Cicero's Philippics attacked Mark Antony and cost the orator his life.
59. The second triumvirate joined Antony, Lepidus, and Octavian legally in 43 BC.
60. The assassins were defeated at Philippi in 42 BC and both leaders died by suicide.
61. The naval battle of Actium in 31 BC decided who would rule the Mediterranean world.
62. Cleopatra VII died in 30 BC, and her kingdom became a Roman province.
63. Octavian took the name Augustus in 27 BC and became the first emperor.
64. He preserved the Republic's offices while quietly concentrating real power in his own hands.
65. He created the Praetorian Guard and a standing professional army with fixed terms of service.
66. Arminius destroyed three legions in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9, ending expansion into Germany.
67. Augustus boasted that he had found a city of brick and left one of marble.
68. The Ara Pacis was dedicated in 13 BC to celebrate the peace his regime imposed.
69. Tiberius succeeded in AD 14 and grew paranoid, eventually governing from the island of Capri.
70. Caligula's erratic reign ended with his assassination in AD 41.
71. Claudius invaded Britain in AD 43 and proved a surprisingly capable administrator.
72. His conquest brought legionary camps, roads, and taxes to lowland Britain.
73. Nero came to power in AD 54 as the last of the Julio-Claudian dynasty.
74. The Great Fire of AD 64 gutted much of Rome, and Nero blamed the minority sect of Christians.
75. He built the extravagantly gilded Domus Aurea across the burned central hills.
76. His suicide in AD 68 ended the dynasty and triggered a year of civil war.
77. Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian seized the throne in that single year.
78. Vespasian restored the treasury and founded the Flavian dynasty.
79. Titus dedicated the Colosseum in AD 80 on the site of Nero's artificial lake.
80. The Arch of Titus still commemorates the Roman storming of Jerusalem.
81. The Jewish revolt of AD 66 ended with the destruction of the Second Temple in AD 70.
82. Domitian ruled fifteen years and accepted divine honors during his own lifetime.
83. Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 79 during Titus's reign.
84. Pliny the Younger's letters describe the eruption and his uncle's death during the rescue attempt off Stabiae.
85. Trajan, born in Roman Spain, became emperor in AD 98 and began the last great conquests.
86. His Dacian Wars brought the gold mines of Dacia into the empire.
87. The Column of Trajan in his forum narrates those campaigns in a continuous spiral relief.
88. Under Trajan the empire reached its greatest territorial extent.
89. Hadrian gave up those distant eastern gains and built a wall across northern Britain.
90. His Pantheon, rebuilt around AD 125, still carries the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
91. The era from Nerva to Marcus Aurelius is remembered as the high point of imperial prosperity.
92. Marcus Aurelius spent much of his reign fighting Germanic tribes along the Danube.
93. He wrote the Meditations as private notes in campaign tents on that frontier.
94. The Antonine Plague swept through the empire from the 160s and killed on a massive scale.
95. The murder of Commodus in AD 192 ended the Antonine line and reopened the civil wars.
96. Septimius Severus, born at Leptis Magna in Africa, founded the Severan dynasty.
97. He reportedly told his sons to enrich the soldiers and scorn everyone else.
98. Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to nearly every free inhabitant of the empire in AD 212.
99. His vast baths in Rome served thousands of bathers at once.
100. Elagabalus scandalized the capital by trying to install a Syrian sun god as Rome's chief deity.
101. The weakness of Severus Alexander helped ignite the Crisis of the Third Century.
102. Between 235 and 284 the legions proclaimed dozens of emperors and promptly overthrew most of them.
103. Maximinus Thrax, the first of the soldier emperors, never set foot in Rome.
104. The empire briefly fractured into a Gallic Empire in the west and a Palmyrene realm in the east.
105. Zenobia of Palmyra seized Egypt and Anatolia before Aurelian captured her city.
106. Some of these emperors ruled for only weeks before being killed by their own troops.
107. Decius launched the first empire-wide persecution of Christians in 250.
108. Valerian became the first Roman emperor ever taken prisoner, handed over by Shapur I of Persia.
109. Aurelian reunified the empire and encircled Rome with a new brick wall.
110. Diocletian ended the chaos in 284 by inventing the Tetrarchy, a college of four rulers.
111. He abandoned Rome as a residence and governed from Milan and Nicomedia instead.
112. His Great Persecution of 303 was the last and the most systematic.
113. He abdicated in 305, one of the very few emperors to leave power voluntarily.
114. Constantine won the civil war after crossing the Tiber at the Milvian Bridge in 312.
115. The Edict of Milan in 313 granted Christianity legal toleration.
116. He refounded Byzantium as Constantinople in 330, shifting the empire's center of gravity east.
117. He summoned the Council of Nicaea in 325 to settle the Arian controversy.
118. Imperial patronage drained away from Rome, and the old city shrank for centuries.
119. Julian the Apostate tried in 361 to revive traditional pagan worship.
120. Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the official religion and suppressed pagan rites.
121. After his death in 395 the empire split permanently between Honorius in the west and Arcadius in the east.
122. Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome in 410, a shock felt across the Mediterranean world.
123. St. Jerome wrote that the city which had conquered the whole world had itself been conquered.
124. Augustine answered pagan accusations by writing The City of God.
125. Rome's population had fallen far below its million-strong peak by the fifth century.
126. Repeated sieges damaged the aqueducts, and many of the city's fountains went dry.
127. Pope Leo I famously met Attila the Hun in 452 and persuaded him to withdraw from Italy.
128. The Vandals of Geiseric plundered Rome methodically for two weeks in 455.
129. The boy emperor Romulus Augustulus was deposed by the Germanic chieftain Odoacer in 476.
130. That deposition marks the conventional end of the Western Roman Empire.
131. Theoderic the Ostrogoth ruled Italy from Ravenna while leaving Rome's Senate in place.
132. Boethius, his minister, wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison before his execution.
133. Justinian's general Belisarius recaptured Rome from the Goths in 536.
134. The Gothic War of 535 to 554 ruined the city and cut its aqueducts.
135. Gregory the Great became pope in 590 and took over the defense, food supply, and diplomacy of the city.
136. The Lombard invasions left Byzantine Italy split into fragments around Ravenna, Rome, and the south.
137. Charlemagne was crowned emperor in St. Peter's on Christmas Day in 800.
138. The Papal States made the pope a temporal sovereign for nearly a thousand years.
139. Medieval Romans crowded down by the Tiber and the Campus Martius while the ancient hills lay overgrown.
140. The Colosseum became a fortress and a quarry, its travertine burned for lime and reused in palaces.
141. The jubilee year of 1450 brought pilgrims flooding back and launched Rome's rebuilding as a papal capital.
142. Nicholas V gathered manuscripts in the 1450s that became the nucleus of the Vatican Library.
143. Bramante, Raphael, and Michelangelo reshaped the city during the High Renaissance.
144. The rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica began in 1506 and took more than a century to complete.
145. Mutinous imperial troops sacked Rome in 1527, ending the Renaissance phase of the city's history.
146. Sixtus V straightened the streets in the 1580s and raised obelisks to mark the pilgrim routes.
147. Bernini's colonnade and Borromini's undulating facades gave Counter-Reformation Rome its Baroque face.
148. Italian troops breached the Porta Pia in 1870, ending papal temporal rule and making Rome the capital of a united Italy.
149. Mussolini's Fascists marched on Rome in 1922, cut grand avenues through the ancient center, and settled the pope's status in the Lateran Treaties of 1929.
150. A 1946 referendum replaced the monarchy with a republic, and the 1957 Treaty of Rome laid the groundwork for the European Economic Community.
